description: Your broad jump is probably not weak, it is sabotaged. Five common mistakes leak distance out of every attempt before your hips even get to work. Take the test, learn what the tape should read, and fix the leaks in order.

scenes.narration: Same test, sharper eyes. Toes behind a line, swing, sink, explode, stick the landing, and measure to the back of your nearest heel. Three jumps, best distance is your number today, and if you can, prop a phone against a shoe and film the best one from the side, because this episode is a fault-finding mission and film does not blink. Keep the number. Last time we measured your broad jump, we talked about the engine, your hip power. Today we talk about the leaks. In my experience a skinny guy's jump is rarely limited by the engine first. It is limited by five small sabotages, technique errors that drain distance before the hips even finish firing, each one cheap to fix and expensive to keep. Most jumpers own at least three of the five. By the end you will know which ones are taxing you, what they cost in centimeters, and the order to fix them in. The tape has been grading your mistakes and calling it your power. Time to separate the two.

scenes.label: THE LINE YOUR JUMP SHOULD REACH
scenes.narration: The line has not moved: two meters separates an untrained jump from an athletic one, and over two forty is elite horizontal power for a bodyweight athlete. What this episode adds is the accounting. Between a sabotaged jump and a clean one, same athlete, same hips, same day, there can be twenty to thirty centimeters of pure leakage: distance the engine produced and the technique threw away. That gap is the size of an entire training season for most guys, available in an afternoon of corrections. So read your number today with two columns in mind. Column one is your engine, the hip power we trained before. Column two is your leakage, the five mistakes ahead. If your distance disappoints you, do not buy a bigger engine yet. First, stop the leaks. Plumbers get rich before engineers for a reason.
scenes.sub: under 1.6 m: check the leaks first - over 2.4 m: elite horizontal power

lines: The jump is a chain: load, swing, blast, flight, stick.
beats.title: FIVE LINKS, FIVE LEAKS

scenes.narration: Before the list, the map it lives on. A broad jump is a chain of five links. You load: sinking and swinging the arms back winds the springs and the hips. You swing: the arms drive forward and the hips begin their blast. You extend: ankle, knee and hip fire in sequence and the ground gets everything you own. You fly: your body travels, legs reaching forward near the end. You stick: heels down, chest up, absorbing without falling. The engine we discussed last time, hip power, lives mostly in link three. But a chain pays out only what its weakest link passes along, and the five mistakes ahead each break a different link: the load, the swing, the aim, the flight, and the landing. That is why fixing them feels like free distance. You are not producing more power. You are finally receiving all of the power you already produce.

Here is why coaches hunt mistakes before building strength: the return on investment is absurdly fast. Muscle and tendon adaptations take weeks to months to move a number. Technique corrections move the same number in a single session, because the capacity was always there, misdirected. Jump research and coaching practice agree on the big leaks: arm swing alone is worth roughly ten to fifteen percent of distance, takeoff angle and landing position each carry their own double-digit percentages, and these stack. A jumper fixing three leaks in a month can gain what a strength block delivers in a season, and the gains do not fade, because motor patterns, once corrected, are kept by the nervous system for free. Your film from the test is the diagnostic tool: watch the dip depth, the arms, the eyes, the flight and the landing, and the mistakes will introduce themselves in order.

The deep dive is the repair order, because fixing five things at once fixes none of them. The nervous system can hold one correction per jump session, so work the chain in order, one link per week. First the load, because everything downstream is built on it: quarter-depth dip, arms sweeping back. Then the swing, violent and forward. Then the aim, eyes and chest up at a target ahead, not down at your feet. Then the landing, heels planted, no backward fall. Film one jump per session and compare it to last week's; the tape measure confirms what the film shows. This patience is not slowness. It is how motor learning actually consolidates, and it is why the guys who fix their jumps permanently look boring for a month and then suddenly fly.

Your advantage in leak repair is practice economics. Technique is learned per rep, and every one of your practice jumps costs your joints a landing force scaled to your light body, so you can rehearse corrected patterns far more often per week than a heavier jumper rationing his knees. Corrections also stick faster on a light frame: less force to reroute means the new pattern succeeds sooner, and success is the only teacher the nervous system fully trusts. And remember the context: the big guy at two meters thirty with perfect technique is near his ceiling. You at the same distance with three leaks open are nowhere near yours. The mistakes are not evidence against you. They are distance you already own, sitting in escrow, waiting for five small signatures.

Now we jump together with one correction in mind: full arm swing, quarter dip, eyes ahead. Four rounds: twenty seconds of broad jumps, stick every landing, walk back and reset. Rest forty seconds between rounds. Quality only, every rep a rehearsal of the fix.

The five broad jump mistakes destroying your hip power. Mistake one: squatting too deep before the jump. A deep dip unloads the springs and stretches the blast window until it goes soft; quarter depth, quick and snappy, is where the power lives. Mistake two: forgetting the arm swing. Arms hanging or drifting politely costs you ten to fifteen percent of your distance, the single most expensive habit on this list; swing them like you mean it. Mistake three: looking down at takeoff. Your body follows your eyes, and eyes on your feet fold the chest and aim the blast into the floor; pick a target ahead and jump at it. Mistake four: landing tall and stiff. Straight legs and a backward fall are measured at your hands and billed to your joints; sink into the landing, heels down, chest tall, and stick it. Mistake five: training jumps tired. Fatigued reps rehearse a slow, leaking pattern and engrave it; jump fresh or do not jump. Fix the five, in order, and collect your escrow.

So, your distance. Read it now with the two columns. If your number sits under one sixty and your film shows three or more mistakes, celebrate quietly: you are not underpowered, you are leaking, and leaking is the fastest problem in this season to solve. One sixty to two meters with clean technique is a genuine engine project, and the hinge work from the broad jump episode is your road. Two meters and beyond with leaks still open means your ceiling is higher than your rivals suspect. Put your distance in the comments, just the number, and if you filmed it, name your worst mistake beside it. Retest in thirty days: same line, same honest heel, one fix per week between now and then. The tape is about to start telling a better story about the same legs.

Thirty days from now, same line, same tape, bring me a longer jump with cleaner film and we will go hunting for the next leak together. Subscribe, and keep your number safe until then. This is {channel}. Train the cable.

title: 5 broad jump Mistakes That Are Destroying Your hip power
